results.title: DigitalOcean jacks up GPU prices 20% — and you'll feel it | Brown Forces Technology Studio
highlights:
# DigitalOcean jacks up GPU prices 20% — and you'll feel it

DigitalOcean just raised GPU instance prices by 20%, effective this week. The increase hits their A100 and H100 SKUs — the same chips every AI startup is fighting over. They're not the only one: Hetzner, OVH, and a handful of others have all lifted GPU rates over the past year. Supply for the good silicon is tight, and the big cloud providers have been pricing it like it's a luxury good ever since the LLM boom.

For a small shop running inference on a single A100, that's a real hit on the P&L. DigitalOcean's original pitch was cheap, ... The market is still hot; prices may move again.

results.title: The State of GPU Cloud: August 2026 Report - Data Storage
highlights:
## Hopper Still Pays the Bills While Blackwell Gets the Headlines

NVIDIA's Blackwell generation (B200, B300, GB200 NVL72) is where the announcements and the marketing budget concentrate. But H100 and H200 capacity, NVIDIA's Hopper generation, still accounts for the majority of production inference workloads running today, and pricing on that older capacity has been falling faster than Blackwell pricing as newer supply comes online.

This creates a genuinely two speed market. Teams training frontier scale models or running the largest inference fleets are chasing Blackwell allocation, often through providers with direct NVIDIA relationships. Teams running steady state production inference, fine tuning, or mid size training runs are frequently better served staying on Hopper, where pricing is now materially more favorable and availability is no longer the constraint it was through most of 2024 and 2025.

The mistake to avoid is treating chip generation as a status symbol rather than a cost input. Match the chip to the workload's actual requirements, then shop that generation across providers rather than defaulting to whichever chip is loudest in the press.

...

Match the chip to the workload rather than defaulting to the newest generation. Hopper (H100, H200) now offers materially better pricing for steady state inference and mid size training, while Blackwell (B200, B300) is worth the premium mainly for frontier scale training or the largest inference fleets where its memory bandwidth is the limiting factor.

highlights:
## The Real Price Range, By the Numbers

As of August 27, 2026, the median on-demand H100 rate sits at roughly $3.39 per GPU-hour across 38 tracked providers, up about 13 percent over the prior 90 days. But that median hides a wide spread: the cheapest verified in-stock on-demand rate runs as low as $1.73 per hour, spot pricing drops to around $0.67 per hour, and reserved commitments (one month) start near $1.53 per hour. At the other end, hyperscaler pricing runs dramatically higher, AWS lists roughly $6.88 to $12.29 per GPU-hour depending on instance type and region.

results.title: Can You Actually Trade AI Compute Prices on Kalshi?
highlights:
Kalshi's GPU compute markets went live in March, letting traders bet on whether the per-hour rental price of chips like the H100, H200, B200, and RTX 5090 will land above or below a given level by a set date. Polymarket launched a smaller version of the same idea. CME Group and Intercontinental Exchange have both signaled plans to build their own compute-linked futures. Three separate exchange operators chasing the same underlying asset within months of each other is usually a sign the market has decided something is real enough to standardize.

Whether the pricing this early actually predicts anything is a separate question, and the honest answer right now is: not really yet.

...

Each contract asks a specific, dated question. As of early August, one live Kalshi market asked whether the average hourly cost to rent an H200 chip over the month would land above or below $5. Like every Kalshi contract, buying the "yes" side at 30 cents pays out a dollar if the answer is yes, and nothing if it isn't, meaning the price itself works as the market's implied probability.

...

This isn't a manufactured market chasing a stable number. Nvidia's B200 chip peaked at $6.11 per hour on May 30 and had dropped to $4.22 by June 21, roughly a 31% decline in under a month. That kind of swing is exactly the sort of price risk a derivatives market exists to help someone hedge, an AI company planning a multi-month training run has real financial exposure to where compute costs land, the same way an airline has exposure to jet fuel prices.

...

Here's where it's worth being honest rather than promotional. Research firm Allium examined six completed weekly Kalshi markets tracking B200 rental prices. Two days before each contract settled, Kalshi's implied forecast was a median of 10% away from the actual final price, while staying within about 2.2% of whatever the spot price happened to be at that moment.

That pattern suggests traders were mostly tracking the current spot price rather than genuinely anticipating where it would move next, closer to following the news than getting ahead of it. That's not a strong forecasting record. It's also not a damning one for a market that had existed for a matter of weeks when the data was pulled, and six contracts is far too small a sample to draw a firm conclusion either way. Compute pricing is also genuinely hard to forecast on its own terms: newer chip generations change efficiency in ways that are difficult to model, which complicates prediction regardless of what market structure is doing the predicting.
